stem:
A 6-month-old boy presents at 2am with 10 hours of vomiting and two loose stools. The early vomits were milky; the last three were dark green. He vomited an oral rehydration trial at triage. He is irritable, with heart rate 165/min, capillary refill 2 seconds, dry mucous membranes and a mildly distended abdomen. His blood glucose is 4.8 mmol/L (3.5-5.5).

Which is the most appropriate management?

options.label: A
options.explanation: NG rehydration suits gastroenteritis failing oral fluids, but bilious vomiting suggests obstruction. Enteral fluid is contraindicated until a surgical cause is excluded.

options.label: B
options.text: Urgent surgical review and IV fluids
options.explanation: Bilious vomiting is bowel obstruction, such as malrotation with volvulus, until proven otherwise. Keep him nil by mouth, give IV fluids, decompress with an NG tube and consult surgeons urgently.

options.label: C
options.text: Oral ondansetron, then oral fluid trial
options.explanation: Ondansetron can help in gastroenteritis, but an antiemetic may mask obstruction. Green vomiting needs surgical assessment, not another oral trial.

options.label: D
options.text: Admit and continue small oral fluid volumes
options.explanation: Continuing oral fluids delays the diagnosis of a possible volvulus, in which the bowel can become ischaemic within hours.

options.label: E
options.explanation: Discharge ignores a red flag. A distended abdomen with bilious vomiting needs same-day surgical review and imaging.

context: Green vomiting in an infant is a surgical emergency until proven otherwise; loose stools do not exclude malrotation with volvulus.
